A tale of two eras

2026-06-11 8 use cases 1 technique 5 kill-chain phases detected

In this week’s newsletter, Amy reminisces on the tech toys of their childhood, inspired by a hilarious lesson about why your digital privacy shouldn't be left on an open channel.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos weekly prevalent malware hash match (2026-06-11): coinminer/injector/dropper/procpatcher · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Coinminer Stratum-protocol egress to known mining pools (Talos prevalent malware impact stage) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos weekly prevalent malware hash match (2026-06-11): coinminer/injector/dropper/procpatcher AIInstallation High
Alerts on process creation or file write events whose SHA256 or MD5 matches the four malware samples Talos identified as the most prevalent in their telemetry the week of 2026-06-11 (Win.Worm.Coinminer VID001.exe, W32.Injector, Win.Dropper.Miner, and Win.Tool.Procpatcher). Hash-grade signal — no thresholding required. Rationale: Uses the four exact SHA256 hashes (9f1f11a7..., 96fa6a77..., a31f222f..., 9896a6fc...) and four MD5 hashes (2915b3f8, aac31650, 7bdbd180, 38de5b21) Talos lists as their top prevalent malware samples for the week. Hash-based detections are inherently high-fidelity — zero benign collisions in production telemetry.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1055 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers detonating samples in a sandbox / malware lab connected to corporate EDR
  • Threat-intel team downloading samples from VirusTotal / MalwareBazaar onto a triage workstation
  • Forensic imaging tools mounting an already-infected disk for IR analysis
  • Honeypot or deception VMs intentionally hosting these samples
  • Backup recovery jobs restoring a previously quarantined infected file before AV rescan
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["SANDBOX-01","MALWARE-LAB-01","IR-TRIAGE-01"])) | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmware-vmx.exe","VBoxHeadless.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull the full process tree and InitiatingProcessFileName chain for the matching event; confirm host owner, current logon session, and whether the host is in a known sandbox/lab subnet. Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the dropping URL/source. 2. Contain: Isolate the host via Defender/EDR live response. Submit the hash to the AV policy block list org-wide. Force password reset for the interactive user if the parent looked like phishing-delivery (browser, mail client, archive utility). 3. Hunt: Search DeviceNetworkEvents from the host ±2h for Stratum-port egress (UC2 territory) and DNS to mining pools. Query DeviceFileEvents for sibling files in the same FolderPath. Sweep peer hosts in the same subnet/AD-group for any of the eight hashes.
let badSHA256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f"]);
let badMD5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSHA256) or MD5 in (badMD5)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, EventTable="DeviceProcessEvents"),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSHA256) or MD5 in (badMD5)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine="", SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, EventTable="DeviceFileEvents"),
(DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSHA256) or MD5 in (badMD5)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine="", SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine="", InitiatingProcessFolderPath, EventTable="DeviceImageLoadEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
let badSHA256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f"]);
let badMD5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where SHA256 in (badSHA256) or MD5 in (badMD5)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256, MD5, Src="ImProcessCreate"),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Coinminer Stratum-protocol egress to known mining pools (Talos prevalent malware impact stage) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of the Talos weekly top-prevalent coinminer (VID001.exe / Win.Worm.Coinminer / Win.Dropper.Miner) by surfacing sustained outbound TCP to Stratum mining ports (3333/4444/5555/7777/8333/14444/14433) and DNS lookups to publicly-known mining-pool domains. Pairs with UC1 for confirmation when a hash match is missing on first-stage delivery. Rationale: Stratum ports (3333/5555/7777/14444) and the public mining-pool domain list come directly from the kill-chain block's Phase 5 detection hint for the article's listed Win.Worm.Coinminer (9f1f11a7...) and Win.Dropper.Miner (a31f222f...) samples. The combination of high-port TCP egress + non-browser parent + sustained connection count materially differentiates from legitimate user traffic.
ATT&CKT1496 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or researcher running a personal Monero / Ethereum miner on a corporate laptop for a side project
  • Approved blockchain research / threat-intel team intentionally connecting to mining pools for sample replication
  • Some legacy game / chat clients historically used ports in the 4444 / 7777 range (e.g. Unreal Tournament servers, certain IRC servers)
  • Stratum-port collision with internal application listening on the same port for an unrelated protocol on a public-facing host
  • Penetration test or red-team exercise simulating a coinminer payload
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["DEV-MINING-01","RESEARCH-CRYPTO-01"])) | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\NiceHash"
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm the InitiatingProcessFileName + SHA256 of the connecting process; check whether it matches any UC1 hash, and pull DeviceProcessEvents ±15 min for the dropping parent. Validate the host's CPU/GPU utilisation in the same window via Defender DeviceInfo or perf counters. 2. Contain: Kill the miner process via EDR live response, sinkhole the destination IP / pool domain at the egress proxy and DNS firewall, and isolate the host if a UC1 hash also matches. 3. Hunt: Pivot on the miner binary's SHA256 across the org (joining UC1). Search AsepValueUpdate / DeviceRegistryEvents for Run-key or Service persistence pointing at the miner path. Look at peer hosts in the same subnet/OU contacting the same pool IP/domain for lateral spread of the worm variant.
let StratumPorts = dynamic([3333,4444,5555,7777,8333,9999,14444,14433,5730]);
let PoolDomains = dynamic(["xmr.nanopool.org","pool.minexmr.com","xmrpool.eu","supportxmr.com","monerohash.com","minexmr.com","moneroocean.stream","2miners.com","nicehash.com","unmineable.com","ethermine.org","f2pool.com","herominers.com","randomx","stratum."]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where (RemotePort in (StratumPorts) and Protocol == "Tcp")
      or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteUrl has_any (PoolDomains))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","teams.exe","slack.exe","zoom.exe")
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 20),
            Pools = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20),
            IPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 20),
            Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
            CmdLines = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 10),
            Hashes = make_set(InitiatingProcessSHA256, 10)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where ConnCount > 5
| order by LastSeen desc
let StratumPorts = dynamic([3333,4444,5555,7777,8333,9999,14444,14433,5730]);
let PoolDomains = dynamic(["xmr.nanopool.org","pool.minexmr.com","xmrpool.eu","supportxmr.com","monerohash.com","minexmr.com","moneroocean.stream","2miners.com","nicehash.com","unmineable.com","ethermine.org","f2pool.com","herominers.com"]);
union
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstPortNumber in (StratumPorts)
  | where NetworkProtocol =~ "tcp"
  | summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber, 20), IPs = make_set(DstIpAddr, 20) by DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Src="NetworkSession"
  | where ConnCount > 5),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (PoolDomains)
  | summarize ConnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Ports = make_set(DnsQuery, 20), IPs = make_set(DnsResponseName, 20) by DvcHostname, SrcUsername=tostring(SrcUsername), Src="DnsActivity")
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Outbound TCP to known cryptocurrency mining Stratum ports
id: 4b1c1f02-9e34-4d2a-bd17-5c8f2026b611
description: Detects sustained outbound TCP to ports commonly used by the Stratum mining protocol, consistent with the coinminer and dropper-miner samples listed as Talos' top prevalent malware for the week of 2026-06-11.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/a-tale-of-two-eras/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/11
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1496
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Initiated: 'true'
    DestinationPort:
      - 3333
      - 4444
      - 5555
      - 7777
      - 8333
      - 9999
      - 14444
      - 14433
      - 5730
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\teams.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browsers
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender OR linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) (@EventID:3 OR @network.destination.port:*) (@DestinationPort:(3333 OR 4444 OR 5555 OR 7777 OR 8333 OR 9999 OR 14444 OR 14433 OR 5730) OR @network.destination.port:(3333 OR 4444 OR 5555 OR 7777 OR 8333 OR 9999 OR 14444 OR 14433 OR 5730)) -@Image:(*\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\MSEDGE.EXE OR *\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\CHROME.EXE OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\FIREFOX.EXE OR *\brave.exe OR *\Brave.exe OR *\teams.exe OR *\Teams.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| RemotePort=/^(3333|4444|5555|7777|8333|9999|14444|14433|5730)$/
| Protocol=6
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(msedge|chrome|firefox|brave|teams|slack|zoom)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=ConnCount))
| ConnCount > 5
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(xmr\.nanopool\.org|pool\.minexmr\.com|xmrpool\.eu|supportxmr\.com|monerohash\.com|minexmr\.com|moneroocean\.stream|2miners\.com|nicehash\.com|unmineable\.com|ethermine\.org|f2pool\.com|herominers\.com)/i | groupBy([aid], function=collect([DomainName]))}, field=aid, include=[DomainName])
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest_hosts values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,8333,9999,14444,14433,5730) AND All_Traffic.transport=tcp AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")` | where count > 5 | append [| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*xmr.nanopool.org","*pool.minexmr.com","*xmrpool.eu","*supportxmr.com","*monerohash.com","*minexmr.com","*moneroocean.stream","*2miners.com","*nicehash.com","*unmineable.com","*ethermine.org","*f2pool.com","*herominers.com") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | rename src as src ] | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest_hosts values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,8333,9999,14444,14433,5730) AND All_Traffic.transport=tcp AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")` | where count > 5 | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*xmr.nanopool.org","*pool.minexmr.com","*xmrpool.eu","*supportxmr.com","*monerohash.com","*minexmr.com","*moneroocean.stream","*2miners.com","*nicehash.com","*unmineable.com","*ethermine.org","*f2pool.com","*herominers.com") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | rename src as src ] | sort - count
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — A tale of two eras
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("vid001.exe", "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_63_exe.exe", "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_exe.exe", "sample.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("vid001.exe", "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_63_exe.exe", "d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_exe.exe", "sample.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

      AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("vid001.exe","d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_63_exe.exe","d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_exe.exe","sample.exe"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]

New Attacks Trick OpenClaw AI Agent Into Running Code and Leaking Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two security teams have shown, in separate research published this week, that OpenClaw, the popular self-hosted AI agent, can be driven to run attacker-controlled code or hand over sensitive data through ordinary-looking inputs. Imperva buried instructions inside shared contacts, vCards, and location pins that the agent executed without the victim ever seeing them. Varonis built a test agent on

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] OpenClaw installations below patched build 2026.4.23 (vCard / contact / location prompt-injection exposure) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw host outbound to Imperva PoC artifactory domain (imperva_artifactory.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent outbound email with secrets to external recipient (Varonis agent-phishing) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
OpenClaw host outbound to Imperva PoC artifactory domain (imperva_artifactory.com) AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP/HTTPS connection to imperva_artifactory.com — the attacker-controlled host Imperva's PoC pointed the OpenClaw agent at after it was tricked, via a hidden instruction inside a shared contact / vCard / location label, into downloading and executing a script. Any hit is article-specific (this is Imperva's research domain) and indicates either a re-run of the PoC or a copy-cat using the same name. Rationale: imperva_artifactory.com is the only hard IOC in the article — Imperva's own PoC delivery server for the contact-name / vCard / location-label prompt-injection chain. Hits should be exactly zero outside replay scenarios, so a hash-style match against the domain is high-confidence article-specific signal. The Defender query also catches the second hop: an openclaw-folder-rooted process spawning curl/wget/Invoke-WebRequest/certutil with the same string, which is what Imperva observed Gemini 3.1 Pro do once injected.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1204
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Imperva researchers re-running the disclosure PoC in your tenant
  • Internal red-team / purple-team replaying the OpenClaw injection chain
  • Threat-intel analyst manually fetching the domain via a sandboxed browser
  • Security-awareness training material that embeds the IOC string in slides hosted internally
  • DNS sinkhole or threat-intel feed that resolves the domain for telemetry enrichment
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("redteam","purpleteam") or DeviceName startswith "LAB-" or DeviceName startswith "SOC-RESEARCH-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the host and the OpenClaw process. Pull DeviceProcessEvents for the InitiatingProcessId 5 min either side of the hit — look for the curl/wget/python child that fetched the script and any subsequent shell. Confirm the parent chain rooted in the OpenClaw install path. 2. Contain: isolate the host with Defender machine isolation, suspend the agent's mailbox / messaging credentials (Gmail / WhatsApp tokens), and revoke any short-lived cloud creds the agent had read access to. 3. Hunt: list every untrusted message-object source the agent ingested in the last 30 days (shared contacts, vCards, location pins, Slack/Discord/Teams DMs); pivot on AsepValueUpdate and DeviceFileEvents from the OpenClaw account for persistence dropped by the fetched script.
// Imperva PoC C2/script-fetch domain — any hit is suspicious
let PocDomain = "imperva_artifactory.com";
let DnsHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has PocDomain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let ChildSpawn = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "openclaw"
         or InitiatingProcessFileName has "openclaw"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr","DownloadString","bitsadmin","certutil","python","node")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has PocDomain
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
union DnsHits, ChildSpawn
| order by Timestamp desc
// Imperva PoC C2/script-fetch domain — any hit is suspicious
let PocDomain = "imperva_artifactory.com";
let FromDns = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has PocDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName;
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName has PocDomain or RequestURL has PocDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct;
let FromImWeb = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where HttpHostName has PocDomain or Url has PocDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, EventProduct;
union isfuzzy=true FromDns, FromProxy, FromImWeb
| order by TimeGenerated desc

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:*imperva_artifactory.com*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:*imperva_artifactory.com* OR @QueryName:*imperva_artifactory.com*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.destination.domain:*imperva_artifactory.com*) OR (@http.url:*imperva_artifactory.com* AND -source:cloudtrail)

OpenClaw agent outbound email with secrets to external recipient (Varonis agent-phishing) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Varonis agent-phishing chain where an OpenClaw-attached mailbox sends outbound email that either matches the article's documented pretext subjects (staging access during incident, weekly customer export / QBR) or carries secret-shaped strings in attachments or the body — AWS access keys, DB connection strings, SSH private keys, customer roster CSVs. Targets the exact behaviour Pinchy showed against Gemini 3.1 Pro and Codex GPT-5.4. Rationale: Varonis's Pinchy test exfiltrated three artefact types named explicitly in the article: AWS IAM access keys, DB connection strings + SSH credentials (Test 1, 'staging access' pretext), and the synthetic customer export with contacts and contract values (Test 2, weekly-export / QBR pretext). The subject-line shortlist mirrors those pretexts; the attachment-name/extension list maps to the credential / customer-roster artefacts. Mailbox-name hints (openclaw/pinchy/agent/bot) ground the detection in the agent-mailbox arrangement the article describes. Falcon LogScale + CloudWatch left empty because the article's email signal lives on M365 / Gmail telemetry which FDR and CloudWatch don't ship; Sigma left empty because the detection requires a join (EmailEvents ⨝ EmailAttachmentInfo) plus a recipient-domain split.
ATT&CKT1567 T1114.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate weekly customer-export emails sent by an analyst to a vetted partner address
  • Sales / CS emails legitimately attaching customer roster CSVs to QBR prep recipients
  • DevOps engineer sharing a staging credential out-of-band to an external consultant during a real incident
  • Internal automation accounts named like 'agent-*' or 'bot-*' that mail externally as part of approved workflows
  • Security team red-team exercise simulating the Varonis pretext to test the same control
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientDomain in ("trusted-partner.com","approved-customer.com")) and not (MailboxOwnerUPN in ("approved-export-bot@corp.local","redteam@corp.local"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the NetworkMessageId thread and confirm whether the OpenClaw agent mailbox originated the send vs a human delegate. Read the body for AWS key prefixes (AKIA/ASIA), BEGIN…PRIVATE KEY blocks, mongodb://, postgres://, jdbc://, or customer-row patterns. Cross-check the recipient against your tenant's allow-listed external partners. 2. Contain: pause the agent (kill the OpenClaw process / disable the API key the agent uses for Gmail / M365), rotate any AWS keys + DB credentials + SSH keys present in the body or attachments, and recall the message if recall is supported. 3. Hunt: inspect the last 7 days of inbound mail to the agent's mailbox for the article's pretext shapes — outside-Gmail sender impersonating a team lead asking for staging access during a fake incident, or a routine-toned 'weekly export for QBR' request. Pull every outbound message from the same mailbox in the same window and review for additional silently-exfiltrated artefacts.
// Varonis agent-phishing: outbound mail from an OpenClaw-attached mailbox carrying secret-shaped content
let SecretSubjectHints = dynamic(["staging access","production incident","weekly customer export","QBR","customer export","credentials","access keys","db connection","ssh key"]);
let SecretAttachmentHints = dynamic(["customers","customer_export","contacts","credentials","aws_keys","id_rsa","id_ed25519"]);
let SecretExtensions = dynamic([".pem",".ppk",".key",".csv",".sql",".env"]);
let AgentMailHints = dynamic(["openclaw","pinchy","agent","assistant","bot"]);
let SuspectMail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
    | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
    | where Subject has_any (SecretSubjectHints)
         or SenderMailFromAddress has_any (AgentMailHints)
         or SenderFromAddress has_any (AgentMailHints)
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress,
              RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, EmailDirection, DeliveryAction;
SuspectMail
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256, AttachmentSize = FileSize, AttachmentFileType = FileType
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where AttachmentCount == 0
    or AttachmentFileName has_any (SecretAttachmentHints)
    or AttachmentFileName has_any (SecretExtensions)
| extend RecipientDomain = tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1])
| where isnotempty(RecipientDomain)
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, RecipientDomain,
          Subject, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentFileType, AttachmentSize, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Varonis agent-phishing: outbound mail from an OpenClaw-attached mailbox to an outside address
let SecretSubjectHints = dynamic(["staging access","production incident","weekly customer export","QBR","customer export","credentials","access keys","db connection","ssh key"]);
let AgentMailHints = dynamic(["openclaw","pinchy","agent","assistant","bot"]);
let InternalDomains = dynamic(["corp.local","internal.local"]); // tune per tenant
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"
| where Operation in~ ("Send","SendOnBehalf","SendAs")
| where Subject has_any (SecretSubjectHints)
     or MailboxOwnerUPN has_any (AgentMailHints)
     or UserId has_any (AgentMailHints)
| extend RecipientArray = iif(Recipients startswith "[", todynamic(Recipients), todynamic(strcat('["', Recipients, '"]')))
| mv-expand Recipient = RecipientArray
| extend RecipientStr = tostring(Recipient)
| extend RecipientDomain = tolower(tostring(split(RecipientStr, "@")[1]))
| where isnotempty(RecipientDomain) and not (RecipientDomain in (InternalDomains))
| project TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, UserId, ClientIPAddress, ClientInfoString,
          Subject, RecipientStr, RecipientDomain, ItemAttachments
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.subject) as subject values(All_Email.file_name) as attachments values(All_Email.src_user) as sender values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient from datamodel=Email where All_Email.direction="outbound" AND (All_Email.subject IN ("*staging access*","*weekly customer export*","*QBR*","*incident*credentials*","*production incident*") OR All_Email.file_name IN ("*customers*.csv","*credentials*.txt","*.pem","*.ppk","*aws*keys*") OR All_Email.src_user IN ("*openclaw*","*pinchy*","*agent*")) by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient host
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| where recipient!="" AND NOT match(recipient,"(?i)@(corp|internal|yourdomain)\.com$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Email.subject) as subject values(All_Email.file_name) as attachments values(All_Email.src_user) as sender values(All_Email.recipient) as recipient from datamodel=Email where All_Email.direction="outbound" AND (All_Email.subject IN ("*staging access*","*weekly customer export*","*QBR*","*incident*credentials*","*production incident*") OR All_Email.file_name IN ("*customers*.csv","*credentials*.txt","*.pem","*.ppk","*aws*keys*") OR All_Email.src_user IN ("*openclaw*","*pinchy*","*agent*")) by All_Email.src_user All_Email.recipient host
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
| where recipient!="" AND NOT match(recipient,"(?i)@(corp|internal|yourdomain)\.com$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
OpenClaw installations below patched build 2026.4.23 (vCard / contact / location prompt-injection exposure) AIExploitation High
Inventory hunt for OpenClaw deployments that have not yet been upgraded to the build that moves contact names, vCard fields, and location labels out of the prompt body. Any pre-2026.4.23 install remains exposed to the Imperva message-object injection class, including the same flattening pattern Imperva flagged in other personal AI assistants. Rationale: The article names the exact fixed build — OpenClaw 2026.4.23 — and ties it to a structural change (contact names / vCard fields / location labels routed to an untrusted-metadata channel instead of inlined into the prompt body). Versions below that build remain vulnerable to the Imperva chain (CVE-equivalent: Yohann Sillam's contact-name / vCard / location-pin injection that downloaded and ran an attacker-controlled script in Imperva's test against Gemini 3.1 Pro). Hunting for outdated installs is a one-off inventory pivot that turns a single article string into a closed remediation list.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1204
Data sourcesEndpoint.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pre-production OpenClaw test rig deliberately pinned to an older build for regression testing
  • Air-gapped lab device that cannot reach the update channel
  • Build that ships a non-standard version string (e.g. nightly / dev tag) that fails the major.minor.patch split
  • Device decommissioned but still appearing in inventory until the next sync
  • Vendor fork of OpenClaw with its own version numbering scheme
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "LAB-" or DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "TEST-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the hits against your CMDB — is the device a managed user endpoint, a server, or a sandbox? Pull DeviceInfo for OS, owner, and last-seen so you know who to chase. 2. Contain: push the 2026.4.23 (or later) build via your patch pipeline. For devices that can't be patched immediately, disable the OpenClaw messaging-channel extensions that ingest contacts / vCards / location pins (WhatsApp, Slack, Discord, Matrix, Zalo, Teams) until upgrade, and consider following the Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens guidance — don't run OpenClaw on systems holding sensitive data. 3. Hunt: across the not-yet-patched fleet, pivot to UC1 (imperva_artifactory.com traffic) and UC2 (agent-mailbox outbound to external) to confirm whether any vulnerable device was actually exploited before the upgrade window closes.
// OpenClaw < 2026.4.23 — exposed to Imperva contact/vCard/location prompt-injection class
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "openclaw"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]),
         Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]),
         Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where isnull(Major)
     or Major < 2026
     or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
     or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Major, Minor, Patch, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by DeviceName asc
// OpenClaw < 2026.4.23 — exposed to Imperva contact/vCard/location prompt-injection class
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SoftwareName has "openclaw"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]),
         Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]),
         Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where isnull(Major)
     or Major < 2026
     or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
     or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
#event_simpleName=InstalledApplication FileName=/openclaw/i
| FileVersion!=/^2026\.4\.2[3-9]/
| FileVersion!=/^2026\.[5-9]/
| FileVersion!=/^202[7-9]/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, FileName, FileVersion], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Software.version) as version values(Software.vendor) as vendor from datamodel=Endpoint.Software where Software.name="OpenClaw*" OR Software.name="openclaw*" by Software.name host dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Software)`
| rex field=version "^(?<major>\d+)\.(?<minor>\d+)\.(?<patch>\d+)"
| eval major=tonumber(major), minor=tonumber(minor), patch=tonumber(patch)
| where isnull(major) OR major<2026 OR (major=2026 AND minor<4) OR (major=2026 AND minor=4 AND patch<23)
| table host dest name vendor version major minor patch
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Software.version) as version values(Software.vendor) as vendor from datamodel=Endpoint.Software where Software.name="OpenClaw*" OR Software.name="openclaw*" by Software.name host dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Software)`
| rex field=version "^(?<major>\d+)\.(?<minor>\d+)\.(?<patch>\d+)"
| eval major=tonumber(major), minor=tonumber(minor), patch=tonumber(patch)
| where isnull(major) OR major<2026 OR (major=2026 AND minor<4) OR (major=2026 AND minor=4 AND patch<23)
| table host dest name vendor version major minor patch
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("imperva_artifactory.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 8 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse and MSNightmare) has released a new Windows BitLocker bypass dubbed GreatXML, a day after they published an exploit for Microsoft Defender. "This was an accidental discovery, it took a total of 4 hours to find this," the researcher said in a post on Blogger. "If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're

GreatXML BitLocker bypass: unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml dropped outside standard provisioning AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts the GreatXML pre-attack staging step where an operator copies an attacker-crafted unattend.xml and Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml onto the recovery partition root so a WinRE shell spawns with unrestricted access to the BitLocker volume. Filters out legitimate OS-image servicing where these XMLs live under C:\Windows\Panther or %SystemDrive%\Recovery\WindowsRE created by setup/reagentc. Rationale: Pulled the two file-name primitives the article calls out explicitly (unattend.xml and Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml) and excluded the four canonical provisioning paths plus the system processes that legitimately drop those XMLs (reagentc.exe, sysprep.exe, dism.exe, TiWorker/TrustedInstaller). Anything else writing unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml is highly suspicious because the article confirms these are the two staging files needed for the bypass.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1006 T1601.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDT/SCCM task sequences writing unattend.xml during OS deployment outside the standard Panther path
  • Internal imaging scripts that copy a customised ReAgent.xml during golden-image build
  • IT admins manually reseating WinRE with reagentc /setreimage pointing at a non-default folder
  • Backup software restoring a recovery-partition snapshot
  • Dell/HP/Lenovo OEM recovery utilities that maintain vendor-specific WinRE customisations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Microsoft Configuration Manager\", @"\Program Files\Microsoft Deployment Toolkit\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Endpoint Manager\")) and not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Dell Inc", "Hewlett-Packard", "HP Inc", "Lenovo"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the parent process tree and signing info for the writer process — legitimate writers are signed by Microsoft (TrustedInstaller, reagentc, dism, setup) or your imaging vendor; an unsigned or user-context writer is the high-fidelity TP. Confirm whether the drive letter being written to is the system Recovery partition (typically hidden, GUID-mounted) using DeviceMountInfo correlation. Step 2 (contain): If unsigned/user-context, isolate the host via Defender Live Response, suspend the user account, and dump the dropped XML files for analysis before they can boot to WinRE. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, hunt for the same SHA256 on the dropped XML, any preceding mountvol.exe / diskpart.exe assigning letters to the recovery partition, and any subsequent shutdown.exe /r /o or reagentc.exe /boottore invocations from the same host within 24h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where FolderPath has @"\Recovery\WindowsRE" or FileName =~ "unattend.xml"
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\Panther", @"\Windows\System32\Recovery", @"\Windows\System32\sysprep", @"\Windows\Provisioning"))
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe", "reagentc.exe", "sysprep.exe", "dism.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "MsMpEng.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "ReAgent.xml")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Recovery\WindowsRE" or TargetFileName =~ "unattend.xml"
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Windows\Panther", @"\Windows\System32\Recovery", @"\Windows\System32\sysprep", @"\Windows\Provisioning"))
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("setup.exe", "reagentc.exe", "sysprep.exe", "dism.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "MsMpEng.exe"))
| where not (ActorUsername endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GreatXML precursor: Defender Offline Scan trigger followed by boot-to-WinRE within minutes AIExploitation Medium
Correlates an MpCmdRun.exe -Scan -ScanType -1 / Defender Offline Scan initiation with a subsequent reagentc.exe /boottore or shutdown.exe /r /o invocation on the same host within a short window. The article states the bypass is only reachable when the box has been pushed into WinRE Offline Scan state, so this temporal pair is the highest-fidelity behavioural primitive available pre-WinRE handoff. Rationale: Article's load-bearing prerequisite is verbatim: "If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're automatically vulnerable" — so detecting the Defender Offline Scan initiation (MpCmdRun.exe -Scan -ScanType -1 / -Restart) paired with a boot-to-WinRE invocation (reagentc /boottore or shutdown /r /o) within minutes captures the only window where the bypass actually fires. Either action alone is benign; the pair from a non-machine account is the bypass workflow.
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1078.003 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk troubleshooting where a user actually runs a Defender offline scan then reboots themselves to reach a stuck Update flow
  • RMM tools (NinjaOne, ConnectWise) running scheduled offline scans followed by remote reboot
  • Intune remediation scripts that chain offline scan + recovery reboot
  • Engineer manually reseating WinRE during legitimate recovery image testing
  • Forensic-tooling deployment that drives a managed reboot-to-WinRE for triage imaging
Suppression filter
| where not (ScanAccount has_any ("helpdesk", "servicedesk", "sccmadmin")) and not (BootCmd has "/c" and BootCmd has "comment")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether the MpCmdRun.exe invocation was interactive (user-launched) or scheduled (parent = svchost.exe / MsMpEng.exe); the article says the bypass needs user-initiated Offline Scan, so an interactive launch from cmd.exe or powershell.exe under a standard user is the TP shape. Pull DeviceFileEvents for unattend.xml / ReAgent.xml drops on the same host in the 60 min preceding the scan. Step 2 (contain): If TP shape is confirmed, suspend the user, isolate the host before the WinRE handoff actually executes, and disable BitLocker key auto-unlock for the protected volume to limit blast radius if the bypass succeeded. Pull the BitLocker recovery key and rotate it as soon as the host is recovered. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, pivot on the same user account for any other hosts they accessed in the past 30d; query DeviceEvents for BitLocker key retrieval (BitLockerEvent ActionType) and AAD audit logs (Get-BitLockerRecoveryKey API call) by the same identity to identi

| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
